title: Giving without a receipt
hookLine: give, and let it go; don't keep score

lines: THE LEDGER IN THE BACK OFFICE.
WHAT HAPPENS AFTER YOU LET GO.
cards: There's a ledger that's easy to keep and hard to admit to. I drove last time. I paid for dinner twice.
I remembered her birthday; she forgot mine. It's not greed exactly. It's bookkeeping.
And the ledger turns gifts into loans: you gave, but somewhere in the back office, it was written down, with a due date.
The giving week ends with the hardest part, the one that decides whether a gift stays a gift: what happens after you let go.

teach.b: In one discourse, Sariputta asks the Buddha why the same gift can bear great fruit for one person and little for another. The Buddha answers with a ladder of motives.
Someone gives hoping to get something back, thinking I'll enjoy the reward of this later. That's a gift, and it bears some fruit.
Higher up, someone gives simply because giving is good, or because it's the family custom, or to follow the example of wise people of old, or because it makes the mind clear and glad.

teach.h: AT THE TOP: AN ORNAMENT FOR THE MIND.
teach.b: And at the top, someone gives as an ornament and a support for the mind. Same rice, same bowl. What changes is what the giver is holding onto.
A later Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, pushes further: a bodhisattva should give without dwelling on anything, not on sights, not on sounds, not on anything the mind could grab.

Later teachers put it as three things held lightly: the giver, the gift, the receiver. Give like a hand that opens and doesn't close again to check what it gave; teachers sometimes call it giving that leaves no trace.
The Pali word for that kind of generosity is caga, which also means letting go, relinquishing. Generosity and letting go are the same word. The week so far: giving first opens the door.
The bowl is open. Glad before, bright during, happy after. Share the last bite.
Attention is a gift. Small and wholehearted.
And the last step: no receipt. Nobody's saying you can't notice who never pays; you can still be wise. But the gift itself, once it leaves your hand, is finished.

how: Some Buddhists give anonymously or without expecting return, and in Mahayana traditions the perfection of giving is described as giving without clinging to the gift, the receiver or the self as giver.

o: generosity that lets the gift go
a vow to give up food for a day
a gift made to get merit back

games.q: match the piece of the giving week.
p: asked why gifts bear different fruit
giving as an ornament for the mind

s: in the ladder of motives, giving to get something back bears no fruit at all
it bears some fruit; the fruit grows as the motive becomes freer.
the Pali word caga means both generosity and letting go
generosity and relinquishing are the same word.
giving without a receipt means you can never notice who takes advantage
you can still be wise; the gift itself just doesn't need a signature.

games.q: Sariputta asks why the same gift bears great fruit for one person and little for another. what does the Buddha point to?
games.why: he describes a ladder of motives, from hoping for a return up to giving as an ornament for the mind.

practice: Bring to mind one gift you're still keeping track of, a favor that wasn't returned or a kindness nobody noticed, written as a line in the ledger, dated.

With the out-breath, imagine tearing up the receipt, not because they deserved it, but because the gift was already complete. Breathe out again, let the hand open, and rest in whatever lightness comes.

wordCard.voice: Caga. Generosity, letting go: giving without a receipt, no score kept, the gift complete the moment it leaves your hand.

orig.note: Pali: generosity, relinquishment; the same word for giving and for letting go.

carryVoice: Your line: no receipt. Generosity and letting go are one word. The giving week ends here.
